sections.name: architecture
sections.value: Three touches around one table. (1) HOT PATH: progress reporting and /status stop asking the whole table; a live-only query hits the partial indexes that already exist and returns in milliseconds; the historical GROUP BY survives only behind an explicit flag. (2) RETENTION: the daemon owns a bounded purge — a store function that deletes done rows older than the window in batches, and a reconciler-style sweep (boot + timer) that calls it and records a receipt in /status and the log. (3) MINT: the dedupe rule extends to failed-non-terminal rows so row 123's duplicate cannot be minted again (a partial unique index or an ON CONFLICT rewrite — if it needs a migration, that is a stop-and-ask, not a fence break). Evidence altitude: EXPLAIN-shape and retention tests with mutations, then PROD — the one-off purge o-prime runs, and the four measurements the profile report took today, re-taken.

value.rationale: One unit, one coder, no PM; o-prime coordinates directly (Jordan, 2026-09-02: dispatch the performance work to agents).

value.inputs: the three owed lists: (1) least confident — can the live-only query miss a state the runner relies on (parked? not_before in the future?); does the purge race a claim (a done row cannot be claimed, but assert it); is the sweep's timer safe under the runner's 32-worker concurrency; does the failed-key prevention change requeue_failed's behaviour (row 123's repair path); (2) disbelieve — re-run both mutations; seed 200k rows yourself; (3) known-open — rows 140/141/124b/122, zero findings.

value.text: A caller of queue_depth that genuinely needs history (the TUI? release notes?) breaks silently when it becomes live-only — the coder greps every caller at ack and lists them
Purging in batches while the runner writes: use `DELETE … WHERE id IN (SELECT id … LIMIT N)` with a short transaction; never a single 1M-row delete on prod

The partial unique index for failed-non-terminal keys may need a migration and a backfill guard for existing duplicates — row 123's repair already removed prod's; the migration must still tolerate them
Retention default of 7 days may be too long for a 1M/day churn — measure today's growth rate and propose a default with a number
